draft.title: Contestability
card: Contestability means the past can be explained in more than one way. This makes history open to debate. An interpretation is an explanation built from evidence. It is not the past itself.

Historians and archaeologists can reach different conclusions about the same past. They may use different evidence, such as texts or objects. They may also use different methods, such as close reading or digging a site.
Historians and archaeologists may ask different questions, give some sources more weight, or fill gaps in the evidence with different ideas. New evidence can also change a conclusion.
A good interpretation is based on evidence and can be explained with it. Comparing interpretations shows how historians and archaeologists reached their views.
draft.remember: Contestability means history is open to debate, because historians and archaeologists use different evidence and methods and can reach different conclusions.

a.q: An archaeologist and a historian study the same ancient site. They reach different conclusions. What does this show about history?
opts: History is contestable, so it is open to debate
One of them must have made up their evidence
Conclusions about the past have no link to evidence
Evidence is useless if experts disagree about it
a.why: History is contestable. Archaeologists and historians may use different evidence and methods, or ask different questions, so they can reach different conclusions. It does not mean anyone invented evidence or that conclusions ignore evidence.
a.clue: Think about what each expert might use and ask.

b.q: Archaeologists thought an Egyptian town was built by a king for his priests. Then workers' tools, bakeries and homes were found. Why might they now revise this view?
opts: The new evidence may not fit the earlier explanation
The earlier explanation was not an interpretation at all
Experts always replace old views with new ones
The tools proved what the king had planned to do
b.why: New evidence can lead experts to revise a conclusion when it does not fit the earlier explanation. Here, the homes and bakeries suggest ordinary workers lived there. Experts do not always replace old views, because new evidence may also support them.
b.clue: Ask whether the new finds match the old explanation.

a.best: History is contestable, so it is open to debate

b.best: The new evidence may not fit the earlier explanation

b.q: Archaeologists thought an ancient Egyptian town was built by a king for his priests. Then workers' tools, bakeries and homes were found. Why might they now revise this view?

Experts may drop old views simply because they are old
The tools may prove what the king had planned to build
